title: Late-Presented & Neglected Infantile Esotropia
summary: A comprehensive guide to the management of large-angle Infantile Esotropia (IE) presenting beyond the critical period. Focus shifts from functional binocularity to reconstructive social alignment, management of secondary motor anomalies, and treatment of persistent amblyopia.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Infantile Esotropia (IE) is a large-angle, stable, idiopathic convergent deviation with onset within the first 6 months of life. 'Late-presented' refers to patients seeking intervention after the 'critical period' for stereopsis (typically >2-4 years of age). In these cases, the goal of treatment transitions from achieving high-grade binocular single vision (BSV) to reconstructive cosmetic alignment and expansion of the peripheral binocular field.

branches: Chavasse's Theory: Mechanical/Refractive obstacle to fusion (Secondary)
Jampolsky: Delayed development of binocular reflexes

sections.title: The Classic Clinical Pentad
content: Large, stable angle of deviation (usually ≥30-40 prism diopters)
Cross-fixation (using the R eye to look L and vice-versa)
Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD)
Inferior Oblique Overaction (IOOA)
Latent or Manifest-Latent Nystagmus (Ciancia Syndrome)

rows: Prominent epicanthal folds; negative cover test; normal Hirschberg.
Inability to abduct; often history of trauma/tumor; smaller angle in primary.
Narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction; limited abduction.
Secondary to poor vision (cataract, RB, optic atrophy).
Indicates long-standing adaptation to avoid diplopia.
Harmonious ARC (Cross pattern with central gap)
Stable sensory adaptation; low risk of post-op diplopia.
Nil or only gross stereopsis (nil at 400 sec/arc)
Functional 'cure' is unlikely; goals are cosmetic.
Increase in deviation angle after wearing prisms
Identifies 'motor instability' and need for larger surgical doses.

sections.title: Mandatory Ocular Examination
content: 1. Visual Acuity: Check for amblyopia (fixation preference or Snellen).
2. Cycloplegic Refraction: Mandatory using Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1%.
3. Motor Evaluation: Prism Under Cover Test (PUCT) at 6m and 33cm.
4. Ductions/Versions: Look for IOOA and V-patterns.
5. Fundus Exam: Rule out organic causes of sensory ET (e.g., Macular scar).

sections.title: Red Flags: Neurological Mimics
content: Inability to abduct beyond midline (Rule out VI Nerve Palsy)
Nystagmus in primary position (Rule out intracranial pathology)
Optic disc pallor or atrophy
New-onset ET in an older child (not IE, check for brain tumor)
Pupillary abnormalities (RAPD)

sections.title: Management Strategy Process
content: Step 1: Correct significant refractive error (Hyperopia > +2.00D).
Step 2: Aggressive Amblyopia therapy (Occlusion/Atropine) until maximal VA or alternation.
Step 3: Surgical planning based on largest stable angle measurements.
Step 4: Address associated motor findings (e.g., IOOA) in the same sitting if possible.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring for consecutive exotropia or recurrence.

content.explanation: U: Updrift of the occluded eye. B: Bielschowsky phenomenon (eye moves down when darker filters placed over other eye). I: Inconsistency (amount of drift varies and does not follow Hering's Law).

sections.title: Ciancia Syndrome (High-Yield)
content: Large angle ET with severe limitation of abduction.
Latent or manifest-latent nystagmus.
Nystagmus 'fast phase' is towards the fixating eye.
Head turn towards the side of the fixating eye to reach the 'null zone'.
Often requires larger medial rectus recessions.

sections.title: Surgical Complications
content: Consecutive Exotropia (XT): Most common long-term risk (up to 20-30%).
Scleral Perforation: Rare but serious (requires cryo/laser).
Slipped or Lost Muscle: Urgent surgical exploration needed.
Post-op Diplopia: Rare in children due to suppression, but a risk in late-adult IE surgery.
Adherence Syndrome: Particularly with IO surgery.

sections.title: Prognosis & Expectations
sections.content: In late-presented IE, the prognosis for 'True Stereopsis' is poor. However, patients often achieve 'Subnormal Binocular Vision' or peripheral fusion, which provides much greater stability than a purely cosmetic result. Most patients require 1.2 surgeries on average over their lifetime to maintain alignment.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Fellows
content: Always measure through the distance correction if the child is hyperopic.
If abduction is limited, use the 'doll's head maneuver' or 'spinning' to rule out VI nerve palsy.
Cross-fixators rarely develop deep amblyopia; if they have a strong preference, suspect an organic lesion or asymmetric hyperopia.
For DVD: Recession of the Superior Rectus is the gold standard; for IOOA: Inferior Oblique myectomy or recession.
In adults with late IE, perform a 'diplopia test' with prisms pre-operatively to ensure post-op alignment won't cause intractable double vision.
